w: Bayern Munich have played here since 2005-06, in a 75,000-seat bowl wrapped in inflatable ETFE panels - the first stadium anywhere with a full colour-changing exterior. It ranks as Germany's second-largest ground, behind Dortmund's Westfalenstadion.
s: Colour-changing ETFE bowl, home of Bayern Munich
_facts: First stadium with a full colour-changing ETFE exterior

w: Home of Aston Villa since 1897, this ground has hosted 55 FA Cup semi-finals - more than any other stadium - and seventeen England internationals since 1899. Built on the former Aston Lower Grounds, it retains the Holte End among its four stands.
s: Aston Villa's home since 1897, FA Cup semi-final king
_facts: Capacity 43,205, home of Aston Villa since 1897
Hosted 55 FA Cup semi-finals - most of any stadium

w: Opened in 1925 as Eintracht Frankfurt's home, this retractable-roof stadium seats 59,500 for league matches, the seventh-largest in Germany. Rebuilt for the 2006 World Cup, it later hosted Euro 2024 fixtures and two 2023 NFL Germany games.
s: Eintracht Frankfurt's retractable-roof ground since 1925
_facts: Hosted 2006 World Cup and Euro 2024 matches

w: Built between 1929 and 1931 for the second Workers' Olympiad, this Leopoldstadt ground seats 50,865 - the largest stadium in Austria. Known as Praterstadion until it was renamed for footballer Ernst Happel in 1992, it hosted the Euro 2008 final, won by Spain over Germany, and remains home to the Austria national team.
s: Austria's largest stadium, host of the Euro 2008 final
_facts: Hosted the Euro 2008 final (Spain beat Germany)

w: Home of Lech Poznan since its 1980 opening, this Grunwald ground seats 42,837 after a 2003-2010 rebuild adding four covered stands. Poland's fifth-largest stadium, it reopened in 2010 with a Sting concert before taking the sponsor name Enea Stadion in 2023.
s: Lech Poznan's rebuilt home, fifth-largest in Poland

w: Arsenal's home from 1913 to 2006, known as Highbury, this ground gained Art Deco East and West Stands in the 1930s. It hosted England internationals, 1948 Olympics football, and FA Cup semi-finals. After Arsenal left for the Emirates, it became flats, keeping the listed stand facades.
s: Arsenal's Art Deco home, 1913 to 2006
_facts: Art Deco East and West Stands from the 1930s
Hosted 1948 Olympics football and FA Cup semi-finals

w: Home of FC Porto since 2003, this 50,033-seat ground is Portugal's third-largest football stadium. Designed by Manuel Salgado to replace the Estadio das Antas, it opened with a friendly against Barcelona, then hosted Euro 2004, the 2019 Nations League final and the 2021 Champions League final.
s: FC Porto's home since 2003, a Euro 2004 venue
_facts: Hosted the 2021 UEFA Champions League final

w: Built in 1999 for the World Athletics Championships and expanded in 2025 to 70,000 seats, La Cartuja is Spain's fourth-largest stadium and the largest in Andalusia. It hosted the 2003 UEFA Cup final between Celtic and Porto, and is now Real Betis's temporary home.
s: Seville's 70,000-seat athletics-turned-football venue
_facts: Fourth-largest stadium in Spain, largest in Andalusia
Hosted 2003 UEFA Cup final (Celtic v Porto)

w: Home of Sheffield United since 1889, Bramall Lane began as a cricket ground and is the oldest major stadium still hosting professional football. It shares with the Oval the distinction of staging an England football international, an England Test match, and an FA Cup Final replay.
s: Oldest ground still hosting pro football, since 1889
_facts: Oldest major stadium still hosting pro football

w: Built between 2017 and 2019 on the site of the demolished Ferenc Puskas Stadium, this 67,215-seat all-seater arena in Budapest's Zuglo district is the home ground of the Hungary national football team. Both the old and new stadiums honour Ferenc Puskas, the Hungarian captain and legend who died in 2006.
s: Hungary's national stadium, named for Ferenc Puskas
_facts: Built 2017-2019 on site of the old Ferenc Puskas Stadium
Home of the Hungary national team

w: Built in 2000 with a capacity of 17,400, this Innsbruck ground is home to Bundesliga club WSG Tirol and Raiders Tirol of the European League of Football. Temporarily expanded to 30,000 for Euro 2008, it belongs to the OlympiaWorld Innsbruck group of 1964 and 1976 Winter Olympics venues.
s: WSG Tirol's home, part of the Olympic venue group
_facts: Home of WSG Tirol and Raiders Tirol

w: Home of Ligue 2 club Montpellier HSC, this 32,900-capacity ground was rebuilt in 1998 from a 16,000-seat stadium to host six matches of that year's FIFA World Cup. It later staged 2007 Rugby World Cup fixtures and group games at the 2019 Women's World Cup. The stadium takes its name from the neighbouring Mosson river.
s: Montpellier's World Cup-rebuilt ground
_facts: Capacity 32,900, rebuilt 1998 for the World Cup
Used in the 2007 Rugby World Cup and 2019 Women's World Cup

w: Home of FC Girondins de Bordeaux and, since 2011, rugby side Union Bordeaux Begles, this ground began in 1924 as a cycle track before its 1938 rebuild for that year's World Cup - the first stadium anywhere with covered stands unobstructed by pillars. Renamed in 2001 for mayor Jacques Chaban-Delmas.
s: Bordeaux's pillar-free 1938 World Cup ground
_facts: Home of FC Girondins de Bordeaux
Built 1924 as a cycle track, rebuilt for the 1938 World Cup
First stadium with pillar-free covered stands

w: Home ground of FK Partizan in Belgrade's Autokomanda district, this football and track-and-field stadium was long known as JNA Stadium after the Yugoslav People's Army, a name fans still use. Converting to an all-seater venue cut its capacity from a former 50,000 down to the current 29,662.
s: FK Partizan's home, once known as JNA Stadium

w: Built as the main stadium for the 1920 Summer Olympics, this Antwerp ground hosted athletics, equestrian, field hockey, football, gymnastics, rugby union and weightlifting, plus a korfball demonstration. Converted to football use afterward, it is now home to Belgian club K Beerschot VA.
s: 1920 Antwerp Olympics stadium, now Beerschot's home
_facts: Main stadium of the 1920 Summer Olympics
Hosted athletics, football, gymnastics and more
Now home to K Beerschot VA

w: Home of ice hockey club Kolner Haie with an 18,500 capacity, this Cologne arena opened as Kolnarena and was, as of 2019, the world's highest-attended arena, selling 699,924 tickets that year. Its roof is carried by a 76-metre steel arch weighing 480 tons.
s: Kolner Haie's arena, world's best-attended in 2019
_facts: Home of ice hockey club Kolner Haie, capacity 18,500
Roof carried by a 76m, 480-ton steel arch

w: Home to Allsvenskan sides Djurgardens IF and Hammarby IF, this retractable-roof arena in Stockholm's Globe City holds 30,000 to 35,000 for football and up to 45,000 for concerts. It meets FIFA and UEFA requirements for internationals, and was formerly named Tele2 Arena.
s: Shared home of Djurgardens and Hammarby, ex-Tele2 Arena
_facts: Retractable roof arena in Stockholm's Globe City
Home of Djurgardens IF and Hammarby IF

w: Home of PAOK FC since the stadium was completed in 1959, this multi-purpose ground in Thessaloniki is owned outright by the club. Its official name is PAOK Stadium, but it is universally known simply as Toumba, after the borough where it stands - a name that has stuck through the decades since the ground opened.
s: PAOK's own ground since 1959, named for its borough
_facts: Owned by the club, named after the Toumba borough

w: Opened 11 February 2024 with an LNB Elite basketball match that Paris won 87-65 over Saint-Quentin, the Adidas Arena in Paris's 18th arrondissement seats 8,000 for sport and 9,000 for concerts. Built as Paris Arena II from March 2020, it also has two gymnasiums for local clubs.
s: Paris's modular arena, opened 2024 with basketball
_facts: Built under the project name Paris Arena II
Includes two gymnasiums for local clubs

w: Built in 1969 and holding 26,354, the Estadi Ciutat de Valencia is home to Levante UD and the fourth-largest ground in the Valencian Community. A 2004 Spain-Scotland friendly was abandoned here after lightning knocked out the floodlights; a 2020 renovation added a new roof and video scoreboards.
s: Levante's ground since 1969, hit by a lightning strike
_facts: 2004 Spain-Scotland friendly abandoned due to lightning

w: Completed in 1994 as part of the Spyros Louis Olympic Athletic Center in Marousi, this 19,000-capacity arena is Greece's largest indoor venue and hosted events at the 2004 Summer Olympics. Panathinaikos B.C. took a 49-year concession in 2023, renaming it Telekom Center Athens in 2025.
s: Greece's largest indoor arena, 2004 Olympics venue
_facts: Completed 1994, part of Spyros Louis Olympic Centre
Largest indoor venue in Greece, 19,000 capacity
Panathinaikos B.C. holds a 49-year concession since 2023

w: Home of Stade Reims, this multi-use ground in Reims has been a World Cup venue twice over - staging matches at the 1938 FIFA World Cup and, eight decades later, at the 2019 FIFA Women's World Cup. It remains the club's main home for league football today, hosting Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 fixtures throughout the season.
s: Stade Reims' ground, a World Cup venue twice over
_facts: Venue for the 1938 FIFA World Cup
Venue for the 2019 FIFA Women's World Cup

w: Home of AEK Athens in Nea Filadelfeia, this all-seater ground opened in October 2022 on the site of the demolished Nikos Goumas Stadium, the newest stadium built in Greece. With 32,500 seats it is the country's third-largest football ground, and hosted the 2024 Europa Conference League final.
s: AEK Athens' new ground, a 2024 Conference League host
_facts: Home of AEK Athens, opened October 2022
Built on the site of the former Nikos Goumas Stadium
Hosted the 2024 UEFA Europa Conference League final

w: Formerly known as Vetra Stadium and then LFF Stadium, this Vilnius ground succeeded the old Zalgiris Stadium as the home of FK Zalgiris, the city's leading football club. It also served as home venue for the Lithuania national football team between 2005 and 2022, and holds 5,067 spectators.
s: FK Zalgiris' home, ex-national team venue
_facts: Home of FK Zalgiris in Vilnius

w: Home of football club Brann since it was built in 1919, this Bergen ground sits at the foot of Mount Ulriken. Its record attendance of 24,800 dates from a 1961 cup semi-final against Fredrikstad, and it now holds 17,317 - the third-largest capacity in Norway.
s: Brann's ground since 1919, Norway's third-largest
_facts: Built 1919, home of Brann ever since

w: Home of FK Zeljeznicar in the Grbavica district of Sarajevo, this ground is occasionally used by the Bosnia and Herzegovina national team as well. It seats 18,434 and carries the nickname Dolina cupova, or Valley of Jars, a name that has stuck to the stadium over the years.
s: FK Zeljeznicar's home, the Valley of Jars
_facts: Home of FK Zeljeznicar in Sarajevo

w: Home of Kasimpasa S.K. in the Kasimpasa neighbourhood of Istanbul, this ground is also widely known simply as Kasimpasa Stadium. Used mainly for football, its capacity was extended to the current 14,234 seats to accommodate the club's Super Lig fixtures throughout the season.
s: Kasimpasa S.K.'s home ground in Istanbul

w: Home of Cardiff City for 99 years until closing in 2009, Ninian Park opened in 1910 on a former rubbish tip secured by founder Bartley Wilson, named for guarantor Lord Ninian Crichton-Stuart. It once held crowds over 60,000 and hosted 84 Wales internationals before shrinking to 21,508.
s: Cardiff City's home for 99 years, built on a rubbish tip
_facts: Home of Cardiff City for 99 years (1910-2009)
Hosted 84 Wales internationals, 1911 to the late 1980s

w: Home of Excelsior's men's and women's teams, this Rotterdam ground was built in 1902 and holds 4,500 - among the smallest stadiums used by a professional Dutch club. One stand is named for Robin van Persie, who came through the Excelsior youth academy from 1997 to 1999.
s: Excelsior's tiny 1902 ground, with a van Persie stand
_facts: Capacity 4,500, one of the Netherlands' smallest pro grounds
Stand named after Robin van Persie

w: Home of Scottish Championship club Inverness Caledonian Thistle, this ground stands in the Longman area of Inverness on the banks of the Moray Firth. Known commercially today as the Sarens PSG Stadium, it hosts the club's home league matches within the Scottish football pyramid year-round.
s: Inverness Caledonian Thistle's ground on the Moray Firth
_facts: Located in the Longman area of Inverness

w: Home of Czech club Slovan Liberec, this all-seater ground takes its name from the Nisa river, which flows directly behind the North Stand. It occasionally hosts Czech national team matches and holds 9,900 spectators; unusually, its oldest grandstand is built directly into a rock face on the site.
s: Slovan Liberec's ground, built against a rock face
_facts: Named after the Nisa river behind the North Stand
Oldest grandstand built into a rock face

w: Used today for Chelsea Women's and Chelsea Under-21 home matches, Kingsmeadow in Norbiton, Kingston upon Thames, was previously the home ground of both Kingstonian and AFC Wimbledon. It holds 4,850 spectators, including 2,265 seats, making it one of the smaller grounds in London football.
s: Chelsea Women's ground, ex-home of AFC Wimbledon
_facts: Home ground for Chelsea Women and Chelsea U21
Formerly home of Kingstonian and AFC Wimbledon

w: Home of Gillingham FC since the club's 1893 formation, Priestfield Stadium briefly housed Brighton & Hove Albion for two seasons in the 1990s. A late-1990s redevelopment cut capacity from nearly 20,000 to the current 11,582 across four all-seater stands, one temporary.
s: Gillingham's home since 1893, once housed Brighton
_facts: Temporary home of Brighton & Hove Albion in the 1990s
Capacity reduced to 11,582 in a late-1990s redevelopment

w: Opened 30 September 2013 with a Rod Stewart concert, this Glasgow arena within the Scottish Event Campus was first named the Scottish Hydro Arena, then the SSE Hydro, before its 2021 rebrand. With capacity up to 14,300, it was Scotland's largest entertainment venue until 2019.
s: Glasgow's arena, opened 2013 with Rod Stewart
_facts: Opened 30 September 2013 with a Rod Stewart concert
Was Scotland's largest entertainment venue until 2019

w: Opened in 1966 and closed in 2013 when replaced by the nearby Tele2 Arena, Soderstadion in Stockholm hosted football and bandy. Its record attendance of 22,000 came in 1982 for a Hammarby IF match against IFK Goteborg, and it staged the Swedish bandy championship final until 1989.
s: Stockholm's demolished bandy and football ground
_facts: Replaced by the nearby Tele2 Arena
Hosted the Swedish bandy championship final until 1989

w: Home of AD Alcorcon in the Community of Madrid, this municipally owned and operated stadium opened with a friendly against Real Madrid on 19 May 1999. It has a capacity of 5,000 and remains the club's regular home ground in the Spanish football league system to this day.
s: AD Alcorcon's ground, opened against Real Madrid
_facts: Owned and operated by the municipality
First match was a 1999 friendly against Real Madrid

w: Opened in February 1926 to host a car exhibition, Forum Copenhagen in Frederiksberg is a multi-purpose indoor arena holding up to 10,000 people. Last renovated in 1996-97, it combines a convention centre and concert hall across 5,000 square metres of floor over two storeys.
s: Copenhagen's 1926 exhibition hall turned arena
_facts: Opened February 1926 for a car exhibition
5,000 sqm of exhibition floor over two storeys

w: Astroballe, also known as L'Astroballe, is an indoor sports arena in the Cusset neighbourhood of Villeurbanne, part of the greater Lyon area in France. Built primarily to host basketball games, the arena holds a seating capacity of 5,556 spectators for its matches and events.
s: Villeurbanne basketball arena seating 5,556
_facts: Indoor arena in Villeurbanne, greater Lyon

w: Inaugurated on 9 November 1986 as Hibernians FC's own ground in Paola, Malta, this was the first purpose-built pitch owned by a Maltese club. It hosted the club's first European match, a 1996 Intertoto Cup tie against Uralmash Yekaterinburg, and is Malta's second-largest stadium.
s: Hibernians' own ground, Malta's second-largest
_facts: First purpose-built pitch owned by a Maltese club
Hosted Hibernians' first European match in 1996
